title: Austrian Postal Savings Bank, Vienna
lede: Otto Wagner’s bank of 1904–1906: a façade of square stone plates held by visible bolts, and a banking hall under a gridded glass vault.
summary: Square stone plates with bolt heads, aluminium details, and a banking hall under a vault of square glass panes. Otto Wagner, Vienna, 1904–1906.

evidence.note: Inspected the Wien Museum photographs (3500 px wide) of a 1908 booklet about the building, Wien Museum inv. 115662/2, which contains photographs of the public entrance and of the banking hall. I did not inspect a modern photograph, so present colours and later changes are not recorded here.

styles.note: A clear example in architecture: the façade and the banking hall are built from repeated squares and grids, with the fixings shown as ornament.

context: Wikipedia: the building was constructed between 1904 and 1906 in reinforced concrete and opened on 17 December 1906; an extension followed in 1910–1912. The façade is covered with square marble slabs; the bolts that articulate it were long thought decorative, but material analysis shows that they secure the thin slabs over a bed of mortar. Wagner used aluminium for the bolts, the portico columns, and the heating fans. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_Postal_Savings_Bank).

The Wien Museum holds a 1908 booklet, “Das K. K. Oesterreichische Postsparkassenamt in Wien”, printed on paper, 23.8 × 15.9 cm, with Otto Wagner named as architect. [Wien Museum 115662/2](https://sammlung.wienmuseum.at/en/object/641443-das-k-k-oesterreichische-postsparkassenamt-in-wien/).
Mia’s label notes that Wagner designed an armchair for the bank in 1904–1906; see [the related model 718 armchair](ref:wagner-armchair-model-718).
observed: In the booklet’s photograph of the public entrance, the lower walls are clad in large stone plates, each marked with round bolt heads at regular intervals; the upper storeys carry a denser field of bolt heads.
The name “K. K. POSTSPARKASSENAMT” runs in one line of thin applied capitals, with small dots after each K.
A flat glass canopy on thin columns covers the entrance; the windows behind it are divided into small square panes.
In the photograph of the banking hall, a curved glass vault is divided into a regular grid of rectangular panes by thin bars, and a flat glass ceiling of square panes covers the side aisles.
The floor is laid in bands and fields of small tiles. Slim cylindrical fans stand along the counters, and a clock and a date board sit on the axis of the end wall.
The booklet page frames each photograph with a border of small open rings, and sets the caption “EIN TEIL DES KASSENSAALES” in capitals between two small open squares.
interpretation: Wagner uses the grid at every scale, from the stone plates to the glass vault, and treats the fixings as the ornament. The building shows the style’s square module without the gold and the figurative motifs of the painters.
The 1908 booklet is itself a small Secession print: a ring border, a centred caption in capitals, and two open squares as end marks.
borrow: Mark a panel with a regular pattern of small dots, like bolt heads, to give it texture without drawing.
Frame an image with a border of small open rings, and close a caption with a small open square at each end.
Divide a large surface into a fine, even grid of thin lines, as in the glass vault.

images.alt: Booklet page with a black and white photograph of the banking hall: a high vault of gridded glass panes over an empty hall with columns, counters, and a patterned floor, framed by a border of small rings, with the caption Ein Teil des Kassensaales.
images.caption: Page from “Das K. K. Oesterreichische Postsparkassenamt in Wien”, 1908, showing the banking hall. Wien Museum, inv. 115662/2, image from the [Wien Museum Online Sammlung](https://sammlung.wienmuseum.at/en/object/641443-das-k-k-oesterreichische-postsparkassenamt-in-wien/), CC0, cropped to the right-hand page.

rights.statement: The Wien Museum releases this image under [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) and asks users to name the author, the photographer, and the Wien Museum. The building is by Otto Wagner, who died in 1918, and the booklet was printed in 1908, so the works shown are in the public domain in Austria and in the United States. The Wien Museum record does not name a photographer.
